messages.subject: Beta preview for rmr 2.0
messages.subject_clean: Beta preview for rmr 2.0
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,
after a summer of relentless development I created a rmr-2.0 branch in preparation for the next release. It is a major release and as such will bring major changes. I also provided a tgz download for people who prefer that route. This build passes most tests with some exceptions in the format support department which I plan to fix later. The documentation (help() ) is now largely out of date and your best bets are reading the tests, which are all updated, and reading the source code, which is much improved in its organization. The overarching goal of this release was to find a synthesis of  vectorized and structured modes so as to bring the API back to its original simplicity while keeping and furthering the advances in speed and structured data support that were achieved with 1.3. The role of lists in the API has been reduced to cases where it's necessary and fewer data conversions should be needed. If you look at the tests you will notice how they have shrunk in number and size not because we are skimping on testing, but because of the simpler API. By simpler I mean a largely objective measure of how many calls and how many parameters to each call there are, but also the more subjective aspect of how simple it is to program against this API. In the next few weeks I will bring the documentation up to speed while trying to incorporate community feedback and tying up a few loose ends. There is a new dependency for rmr, quickcheck, also available for download. It is needed only to run R CMD check and I will try to make it optional before general release (unfortunately I couldn't find any support in R for optional dependencies). If you are familiar and productive with rmr 1.3, I encourage you to try the new version (not in production for now) and let me know what works for you and what doesn't. Thanks

Antonio

On Tuesday, September 18, 2012 4:08:27 PM UTC-7, Srini wrote:
> Hi,
>    I ran the tutorial code from RevolutionAnalytics - wordcount.It ran fine, but I am unable to view the output when I execute the "hadoop fs -text" command (as seen below).

It's a binary format so I don't see this as a highly promising approach. When I want to do bit nitpicking I do a hadoop fs get followed by a hexdump -C. It's not something users would ever want to do. Also the example does not write to that location, would you mind sharing the exact code you run?

> I tried to change the code to force my output.format = "text" and also to "native.text".

That should work.

> No success. Can someone suggest where I am making a mistake? I don't think I must specifically "make" an output format for this simple thing.

No you shouldn't but it's not that complicated either (make.input.format("csv", sep = ",") or some such).

>
> > packageDescription('rmr')$Version
> [1] "1.3.1"

And what Hadoop  please?
>
>
> bash-4.1$ hadoop fs -text /user/srini/rmr/out/part-00000 | more
> 12/09/18 22:52:57 WARN snappy.LoadSnappy: Snappy native library is available
> 12/09/18 22:52:57 INFO util.NativeCodeLoader: Loaded the native-hadoop library
> 12/09/18 22:52:57 INFO snappy.LoadSnappy: Snappy native library loaded
> text: java.io.IOException: WritableName can't load class: org.apache.hadoop.typedbytes.TypedBytesWritable

You may have an older Hadoop that we can handle.

> bash-4.1$
>
>
> bash-4.1$ hadoop fs -cat /user/srini/rmr/out/part-00000 | more
> SEQ/org.apache.hadoop.typedbytes.TypedBytesWritable/org.apache.hadoop.typedbytes.TypedBytesWritable

That's a sequence file, you need to understand the difference between a binary file and a text file or it's going to be tough. To read those try hexdump -C filename | less. But I don't see why you would want to do that unless you are developing a format or something.
>
>
> Thanks,

You are welcome

A

> Srini.

Hi Antonio,
    I am using Hadoop 0.20.2-cdh3u4. And here is the code I am trying to run.

#
# from https://github.com/RevolutionAnalytics/RHadoop/wiki/Tutorial
#

library(rmr)

# Set "LOCAL" variable to T to execute using rmr's local backend.
# Otherwise, use Hadoop (which needs to be running, correctly configured, etc.)

LOCAL=F

if (LOCAL)
{
rmr.options.set(backend = 'local')

# we have smaller extracts of the data in this project's 'local' directory
hdfs.data.root = 'data/local/wordcount'
hdfs.data = file.path(hdfs.data.root, '')

hdfs.out.root = 'out/wordcount'

hdfs.out = file.path(hdfs.out.root, 'out')

if (!file.exists(hdfs.out))
dir.create(hdfs.out.root, recursive=T)

} else {
rmr.options.set(backend = 'hadoop')

hdfs.data.root = 'rmr'
hdfs.data = file.path(hdfs.data.root, 'data')

hdfs.out.root = hdfs.data.root
hdfs.out = file.path(hdfs.out.root, 'out')
}

map = function(k,v) {
lapply(
strsplit(x = v, split = '\\W')[[1]],
function(w) keyval(w,1)
)
}

reduce = function(k,vv) {
keyval(k, sum(unlist(vv)))
}

wordcount = function (input, output) {
mapreduce(input = input ,
output = output,
input.format = "text",
output.format = "native.text",
map = map,
reduce = reduce,
combine = T)}

out = wordcount(hdfs.data, hdfs.out)

df = as.data.frame( from.dfs(out, structured=T) )
colnames(df) = c('word', 'count')

# sort by count:
df = df[order(-df$count),]

print(head(df))

Thanks,
Srini.

I have a use case that consists of applying a classifier to a document-term-matrix (DTM) that is saved in a sparse format on HDFS. In this case the mapper is the identity function and the reducers actually do all the work, processing the data record-by-record. The reason for letting the reducers do all the work is that the DTM has to be sorted first (which happens automatically between the map phase and the reduce phase).

Based on my understanding, this cannot presently be implemented in rmr, even when using combiners.

Now, there is probably a way to rewrite the algorithm such that it also fits into the rmr-style framework, and this rewritten algorithm may or may not be contrived (I have not thought about this deeper). However, to me it seems that the approach in my paragraph above is a natural way of solving this problem.

By the way, I very much like the design of rmr's API in general. I'm just thinking that for some cases it might make sense to be able to write reducers in the usual Hadoop Streaming style (which is also the way RHIPE does it). Thanks.

You are certainly aware that this is not a recommended mapreduce style, independent of the language or library used. You are foregoing any amount of locality by moving the complete dataset across the network.

> The reason for letting the reducers do all the work is that the DTM has to be sorted first (which happens automatically between the map phase and the reduce phase).

The java reduce calls handles one record at time, with sorting guarantees within the partition (if you use the default hash partitioner, you end up with a sorted random subset). The RHIPE reducer, the last time I checked, which admittedly was long ago, takes a subrange of records in this same order at a time, with no guarantee that all the records with the same key will appear in the same call. So it is not the same as Java, it is somewhere in between. At least that's my understanding and if I am wrong I would love to understand the current or correct way things are. Users making the switch from RHIPE have specifically complained about the work it takes to group all the same-key records. It is particularly hard because of the append bug which I had to work around. The streaming style makes sense in Java because it is a relatively efficient language, but with R the overhead of a single reduce call is such that you need to get some real work done in a single call, that's why the grouping was preferred. Sometimes with very large records this motivation is moot and sometimes with very small records and a large number of distinct keys the solution is not enough. So we would need not one or two but three reduce interfaces. We've done something like that on the map side for rmr 1.3 but the added complexity was significant. In 2.0 we are going to bring the complexity down again while keeping all (I hope) of the power gained in 1.3. How to do that in an elegant way on the reduce side is still unclear to me, but it's not a closed door and seeing potential use cases certainly helps.

  keyval(screenName, tweetCount)

Say you have a whole bunch of records of the form (documentID, term, frequency). These records are not necessarily sorted according to documentID. Now, for each document, you want to calculate a table that shows how often a every term occurs in this document. For this, you need to first sort the records according to documentID, and then you can process the sorted records line-by-line, because you can be sure that once a new documentID appears, you have exhausted all the entries that belong to the previous documentID. This is an approach working directly with Hadoop Streaming (no R package required), and here I'm not sure how to do this without letting the reducers do all the work.

By the way, the reducers would have plenty of keys, since the number of keys is the same as the number of documents, which is large. So scalability in this sense is not a big issue, although you are right that it's not good mapreduce practice to move around all the data to the reducers.

And yes, this example would fit perfectly fine with the existing rmr API. I apologize for making such a strong statement about rmr earlier. The reason why I'm writing this post is to answer why in this use case the reducers do all the work and why it is necessary to sort the records. (I guess in rmr the sorting happens behind the scenes before calling the reducer.)
